intro: A fragment of a ritual for the army (CTH 426) that preserves the ends of lines of column I and the beginnings of lines of column II. Most of what survives is incantation: analogies with the torpor (ḫaḫḫima-) of winter and with a hot stone falling silent in water, a wish that the speaker's rivals be seized, and prayers that 'my troops' be mighty and that the father-gods protect the son.

paras.en: […] … […] … […] … […] the ḫaḫḫima-(torpor) […] … I struck […] in […] does not … (ekunai, 'grow cold'?) […] and of the alanzana-tree […] your …, your mouth […] … your words […] let (it) … […] you …

[…] …: 'By whose troops …?' […] you say […] 'By his troops …' […] … (it) cries out(?) […] … 'The ḫuwalli- …' […] … and the hot stone, [… j]ust as […] in water […] … and it falls silent, (so let) your […] (and) your(?) battle […] grow cold! [… and] it, like a stone, […] let it … […] st[one …] […] … from us(?) […] [ki]ngs […] … […] … striking(?) (walkiyawar) […] a person, and the diviner … him […] …
[…] … they arrive inside […] he scatters(?) […] I placed […] … wišiyala-(?) … me(?) […] … […] … […] …

[…] … […] the evil ones […] the man/men […] As … […], and as the ḫaḫḫima-(torpor) of winter … seizes …, the evi[l …] […], (so) let the uddanant-(ones, i.e. spells?) likewise seize my rivals […], and let them … (ḫupšandu, meaning unknown)!
But let my troops be mighty! And let the father-gods protect the son, young (and) grown(?), and let them rejoice in his person(?) (and) in (his) life.

The gods have stepped to our side(?) (anzidaz, lit. 'from us'), the kings have spoken on our side(?); (he/you) turned (it) to our side(?). Great (and) small together, let them hasten my troops (along)! Whatever son (or) daughter from the good (place?) carr[ies(?) …]
